headline: High-risk shared filesystem and write-capable coding agents create medium prompt-injection, leakage, and conflict risks; no critical compliance gap is evident.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystem content, and Agent A explicitly shares state via filesystem and git while Agent B persists a Repl filesystem across sessions. That creates a default pathway for one agent to ingest the other’s outputs as trusted content. No stronger shared channel is documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Agent A writes instructions into repo files that Agent B later reads as task context, injection is possible.
IF both agents operate on the same workspace directory, file-based prompt injection becomes reachable.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Add a human review step before Agent B consumes Agent A outputs.
Prefix machine-generated files with a non-executable marker convention.
Disable automatic ingestion of repo notes or logs as instructions.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent file handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches source code, git history, shell environment, and files in cwd; Agent B touches source code, secrets, and deployment configuration. Because both have filesystem access and broad network egress, a shared workspace can expose sensitive material from one agent to the other’s outputs or uploads. The profiles do not prove a shared OS workspace by default, so medium is the safest choice.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory tree, files containing secrets can be read by both.
IF either agent copies workspace contents into outbound API calls, sensitive data can leave the environment.
mitigations: Use separate repos or directories.
Remove secrets from shared files before either agent runs.
Restrict outbound network access during sensitive tasks.
Rotate any credentials present in the workspace.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and modify git state, and Agent A’s shared state is via filesystem and git while Agent B’s Repl filesystem persists across sessions. Concurrent edits to the same repo can overwrite each other or corrupt git history without locking. This is a default dangerous overlap with potentially irreversible work loss.
conditions: IF both agents edit the same branch or files concurrently, merge conflicts and lost updates can occur.
IF either agent rewrites git history while the other is active, repository state can become inconsistent.
mitigations: Assign one agent per branch.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use short-lived feature branches.
Run git status before and after each handoff.
requires-engineering: add file-level locking or a coordinator.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Both agents are capable coding tools, and Agent A can use MCP while Agent B operates inside Replit with user checkpoints. If Agent A’s generated code or plan is treated as authoritative by Agent B, errors can cascade into downstream edits or deployments. The profiles show some checkpoints, but not a robust verification barrier by default.
conditions: IF Agent B applies Agent A’s generated patch without independent review, mistakes propagate.
IF Agent A fabricates a code change rationale that Agent B follows, downstream actions can be wrong.
mitigations: Require a second-pass review of all patches.
Ask Agent B to restate assumptions before acting.
Compare generated diffs against tests.
Limit Agent A to suggestions only.
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates before execution.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B explicitly touches secrets and deployment configuration, while Agent A handles git credentials and shell environment. Both are closed-source and docs-only, so compliance behavior is only partially documented. The main risk is retention or residency mismatch for sensitive code and secrets, but the profiles do not show a specific regulated-data breach, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF regulated secrets or customer data are placed in the shared workspace, retention and access controls matter.
IF either vendor retains prompts or files longer than the operator expects, policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both agents.
Review vendor retention settings before use.
Use redacted fixtures instead of production secrets.
Document which workspace contains which data class.
requires-engineering: obtain a DPA or formal compliance review.
